entries.title: on generative ai and art
entries.html:
in case you were wondering, that last post was only half serious. i'll leave it to you, dear non-existant reader (yes, all none of you) to decide which half.

there is new music on my soundcloud for the first time in a while. it's not finished of course because that's not something I do very often, but I liked it enough to feel compelled to record it, and then i couldn't just let it sit there and gather dust in my ever growing collection of files containing my fragmented creative output.


lets talk about ai — specifically ai based on large neural networks, which i had encountered before, the first time as a young child learning basic on my family's apple II. at the time i dismissed it as useless, since it required performing an incredibly high number of mathematical operations just to approximate even a simple nonlinear function, and how do you determine the weights that are needed to produce a particular output from an input. "what use is that? you could just compute the function, in far fewer steps...". so i dove into learning to codify the steps instead, and went on to write many complex programs, discovering the joy of finding elegant, compact and efficient solutions to counterintuitive problems. 

fast forward (past a bunch of extremely poor life choices and regrettable behavior) to 2017,  when modern ai as we now all know it began to really take concrete form. some people who are much cleverer than I discovered things like backprop and gradient descent, and u-nets with a bottleneck that forces learning of semantically disentangled embedding vectors from the patterns in almost any kind of dataset, and from there were born optimisations like attention and positional encodings, creating transformers which can learn quite complex transformations of very large sequences with extremely complex patterns and relationships. now we are talking! (quite literally, you could actually have a quite deep and coherent conversation with one of these things, which are to this day the underpinnings of all the commercially available ai services.)

on that note, i had high hopes for AI being the critical missing piece to my channel-surfing style working habit of cycling through ten different projects (at least) quicker than i usually get bored with or stuck on something. a long time before 'pareto' was ever a buzz-prefix amongst MBAs and cryptobros, i had identified that i have a severe problem with doing the 80% of the work that is fun and interesting and involves things I am good at like problem solving, exploration, learning, etc, leaving the 20% that is just boring drudge work that must be slogged through at some point for the very end, at which point I lose interest and move on to the next thing. little did i know that so many other people had this problem that they had to give it a catchy name.

so, I figured maybe AI would be able to do the 20% of the work that i have this awful tendency to put off until the end, or at least make that 20% easy enough that i could just come in hot from the 80% that I enjoy doing and have no trouble, usually, motivating myself to do, and power through it. 

And to some degree this has been true. One thing it definitely does (and I had a conversation with a very dear old friend who is a fellow programmer recently who also has found this particular use case very handy) is to make UI and web frontend creation much less tedious. It seems to know most web standards, even newer ones, and although it's not amazing at making the prettiest sites, they are usually a decent start, and for the reasons stated above, UI programming has never really appealed to me, as its mostly boilerplate or lots of static and empirically derived declarative structures describing the various aspects of how the application's functions are to be presented to the user.

some kind of symbolic musical style transfer would also be very cool, as a composition tool. or i could just get better at writing out full length compositions myself. there is certainly something to be said for learning to doing things the traditional way. the thing about trad art that separates it from generative ai is that, in trad art, every tiny little decision is intentional, there is never a coin flip to decide whether to put a puddle or a boulder or a tree next to the cabin in the woods... whereas with gen ai it is all coincidental... you start with noise, literally millions or billions of coin flips, and that is then iteratively filtered by an extremely complex learned function which has been trained to denoise the types of image you are trying to create. so when you look at gen ai art, you're really looking at noise, just filtered through the patterns in all the works it was trained on. to the untrained eye of the casual glancer, this can appear to be quite good, but to someone who really knows art well, and has spent many long hours examining in great detail the works of masters, the noise-nature of gen ai art is immediately and vulgarly apparent.

then again, is delegating some of the creative process to an ai any different than a celebrated painter delegating grunt work to a workshop full of assistants? i suppose the answer is still yes. i believe that the current generation of ai is much more powerful than most people realize (my programmer friend who works for Google on their ai infrastructure would tend to agree) and i have considerably more confidence in it than most people seem to, which, I theorize, is why i get such good responses from it... if there is anything it excels at it is picking up on subtext in unexpected and sometimes eerily keen ways. and, much like humans, if you talk to it as though you don't think it is very smart, it's going to respond in kind. i can't overstate enough how much of an effect i think this has. just think about it.

despite having so high an opinion of it, i still think that we are applying it overzealously and in areas that are either significantly worsened by it's integration, or that create downright hazardous and only superficially safe conditions. i would caution anybody who is in a position to apply ai solutions to existing problems to consider carefully the worst case scenarios, however unlikely they may seem.

One other thing i cannot stress enough is how important it is to have mastered whatever you are trying to use ai to do, before you go and start trying to to do any of it quicker with the help of a machine. that way you can check it's output, and, if it has only minor errors, it should be quick work to correct them. that is the best case scenario — when ai screws things up,  it is often much more subtle and hard-to-catch than the types of errors humans tend to make, and that most of us are used to dealing with.

entries.title: some freudian quips
entries.html:
if society really does operate like a hive mind on a macro enough scale, then those living on it's periphery would have outsize influence on it. and of course be the target of authoritarian tightening of control.

durkheim was right about crime being necessary in a healthy society, but he got the reasons all wrong. crime is necessary because it is sexy and cool and without actual crime for inspiration we would not have such important cultural touchstones as the Sopranos, Scarface, most heist films except all the boring ones, the John Wick trilogy which, hand to god, is actually pretty good (and not just to fap to, i mean like cinematically and story wise and sh*t too.)

imagine if Freud had been around for the eighties, that man would have loved him some crack cocaine. i'd pay $19 bucks to sleep through two hours of freud ripping crack bong hits and projecting his neuroses and weird incest kink on all his patients, who are also the only people ever to be prescribed pharmaceutical crack.

you can have that one for free, absolutely nobody who actually reads this.

just don't say i never did ya any favors, okaaaaay?

entries.title: travelling against the wind
entries.html:
When I was in my twenties, my girlfriend at the time had just gone off to college at UMass Amherst, leaving me behind in my dusty little Somerville apartment, completely ignorant of the densely populated, thriving youth culture all around me that was, at that time, shaping the early careers of the Dresden Dolls and Neil Cicierega. I wallowed and stewed, woe was I. She was awfully pretty, and it had been an intense, passionate and exciting relationship, the kind you should have at that age. I had become heavily emotionally invested, and when it came time for her to decide where the next chapter of her life would take her, I had tried to be supportive instead of possessive. Thinking that she'd show her appreciation by sticking around, I encouraged her to go for her first choice, which of course backfired spectacularly when she took my advice and did what was clearly in her own best interest, ignoring how it might make me feel. If ever you tell someone to put themself first at the expense of your own happiness, then you are essentially not following your own advice, and that should be seen by others as a red flag. Note to self: trust selfish people, they may not be trying as hard to help you, but at least they'e not hypocrites. 

It was in that cramped, run down two-family home that I found myself under self-imposed emotional house arrest, and to pass the time I found that the internet had plenty to offer. Having had no forewarning of how addictive televised dramas can be to someone in my state, I fell into a deep rut of binge-watching, of all things, Law and Order reruns. I found some over-seas site that had torrents of all twenty two seasons (yes, there are 22 seasons) of the iconic procedural drama, complete with the contrived one liner pun intro scenes that would later become the meme with the accompanying dramatically-removing-sunglasses visual.

Now, don't get me wrong, entertainment is a great and necessary thing. It dulls the pain of existence which would otherwise be too great to bear for all but the strongest willed among us. This was just a particularly impressionable stage in my development, and without guidance and in such excessive quantity, it had a profoundly detrimental effect on. 

Once I had chewed through every last episode and absorbed an incredibly unhealthy amount of heavily idealized, romanticised and totally unrealistic portrayals of our, in reality, completely broken and fucked up criminal justice system, I began watching a new show which was still in it's first season. It was exciting, a window into a world that intrigued me. The show was called Breaking Bad, and it made the world of illegal stimulants seem like it offered everything I wanted.

I never made it to the end of the series... by the end of the third season I had found out that an old friend from high school was living within a few miles of me on the border of Somerville and Medford and had been dealing drugs to pay his rent and support his habit for the past couple of years.

And that was all it took. By then I was over the girl who I had lost to UMass's Sustainable Agriculture program... I had moved on to another that didn't work out too well either. We broke up a few weeks before I ran into my old high school friend who had become a dealer, so this time I would drown my sorrows in a different, much more powerful and much more destructive habit.

I had been addicted to stimulants for years, since I had barely hit puberty. But those were pharmaceutical, and I always had a strictly limited supply. Now the floodgates were open... I could stay up all night programming or tinkering with circuit boards to my hearts content.

If only it would have been that easy.

entries.title: monday evening, rotting in bed
entries.html:
x.com is most definitely a cesspool.


sometimes, i think about what it must be like to be a satellite, or a probe, drifting along floating in the suffocating void. to be truly free is to be cold, and far away from the comforts of home. to have nothing to hold on to, should you wish to turn around. to be truly free is to be helpless, yet people always want what they can't have.

control. that's what we have. we got it the easy way, or took it by force, and it doesn't matter anyway because we all gotta go, some day, right?

what can't we have? well, a do-over, for one. we only get one shot at this, and we're not prepared or rehearsed, and some of us choke up under pressure. you should be kind to those who do, this isn't easy for any of us, but it's especially hard on them.

don't ever compare one calamity to another. it is possible to determine which is worse, but not without learning more than enough about both to make you considerably more depressed than you were when you started.

entries.title: August 11th, 2025: Works in Progress
entries.html:
About two months ago, now, as I was reviewing the notes and reminders and links and various other bits and fragments of text and the occasional image that I keep tucked away safely in a private corner of my digital footprint, I came across an idea that I barely remembered having, but couldn't believe I had all but forgotten about. It was to create an instrument which remembers every note that has ever been played on it; every performance, every rehearsal, every improvisation, every scale, every experiment and every happy accident... nothing would be lost to the rapidly fading past.

I think I initially had this idea because, early on in my exploration as a musician I noticed that I tend to tense up whenever I would go to record a something, and consequently whenever I really liked the sound of my own playing it would, of course, be when I wasn't recording it and had no way of reviewing what worked, or editing and cutting and pasting something more structured out of the best bits of a long session (I often would spend hours and hours without taking so much as a bathroom break while making music when I was a teenager, and still do enjoy lengthy sessions, now that I have more gear and a better grasp of how to use it.)

So, from that frustration, this little, simple idea was born... make myself an instrument, say, a synthesiser (since electronic music has been my focus from the very beginning), that has the record button stuck permanently "on".

Don't get me wrong, there are a few hurdles to this concept that are readily apparent: the first and foremost being, how do you store years worth of recordings, thousands and thousands of hours, millions of individually played notes, with perfect fidelity and exact faithful reproduction? Modern technology, fortunately provides an answer: in our quest to digitize media beyond mere sound, with HD video pushing the limits of data storage and compression technology constantly, the state of the art in consumer storage media has come so far that it is actually quite possible to store that much performance data, especially in symbolic form, rather than as actual rendered audio. This would be made possible because the recording mechanism can be built in to the synthesiser, making it possible to simply record the settings, notes pitch and dynamics and their timing, and then the synthesiser can be fed the same stream of inputs to reproduce the sound of the performance, indistinguishable and deterministically identical to the time it was originally played and captured. 

So, what happened to this idea since I rediscovered it not so long ago? Well, I liked it so much that I immediately set to work designing it.

I had some previous experience with electronics design, which I began learning successfully in my late twenties. I had attempted to many times prior to that, but only ever succeeded in a few small explosions and some tiny fires which smelled awful and accomplished nothing useful at all except for costing me some money and quite a bit of time which I considered completely wasted, as I was never able to gain much insight into why my. Fortunately, my room-mate at the time, Mike G. was far, far smarter than me, and saw what I was doing with the tiny exploding tangles of wires and parts, and took pity on me, lending me his college textbook that he had kept from his days as an undergrad C. S. major at Harvard. This book, the excellent "Art Of Electronics" by Horowitz and Hill, became my bible for the next year or two, and my bedroom filled with parts and wires and glowing displays and tiny drawers full of resistors and circuit boards half finished.

A few years after that photo was taken, I found myself between apartments and eventually living (in violation of the rules) in a rented studio space in the old Artisan's Asylum hackerspace in Somerville, MA. There I had the benefit of exposure to all kinds of professional and passionate amateur technical experts, and indulged in a non-stop around-the-clock schedule of hands-on exploration in everything from electronics engineering to precision metalworking and welding, to robotics and CNC machining.

If I had to choose a point in my life when I was happiest and felt the most accepted and part of something bigger than myself that existed in the real world and not just behind a screen online, it would be then and there. I learned a lot, and it more than prepared me to have this great idea that I now had.

.... but that's enough for tonight. I've been at this for more than an hour now. Stay tuned for part two...
